ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE–DRIVEN 
PREOPERATIVE RISK STRATIFICATION FOR 
EARLY ALLOGRAFT FAILURE IN LIVING 
DONOR LIVER TRANSPLANTATION
Yujin Han* 1, 2, Hangsik Shin1, 2, Dae-Hyeon Won3, Young-In Yoon3
1Department of Medical Science, University of Ulsan, 2Department 
of Medical Informatics and Statistics, 3Department of Surgery, Asan 
Medical Center, Seoul, Korea, Republic Of
Background: Early allograft failure (EAF) following liver 
transplantation remains a catastrophic complication 
associated with substantial early mortality and the need for 
retransplantation. In living donor liver transplantation (LDLT), 
which is founded on the sacrifice and risk assumed by a 
healthy donor, the occurrence of EAF carries even greater 
clinical and ethical implications, representing a particularly 
grave and consequential event. 
Purpose: This study aimed to develop and interpret an 
artificial intelligence–based model capable of predicting 
preoperative risk for EAF in LDLT recipients.
Method: In this retrospective study conducted at Asan 
Medical Center (Seoul, South Korea), we analyzed data from 
4,973 adult LDLT recipients, among whom EAF occurred 
in 148 patients (3.0%). A total of 26 preoperative variables 
were included, including donor and recipient demographics, 
comorbidities, perioperative clinical characteristics, and 
transplantation-related parameters such as the graft-to-
recipient weight ratio (GRWR). The dataset was randomly 
divided into training (75%) and independent test (25%) 
cohorts. An XGBoost model served as the primary prediction 
algorithm, supplemented by an anomaly score derived from 
an Isolation Forest to enhance detection of rare, high-risk 
patterns. Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley 
Additive exPlanations.
Result(s): On the independent test set, the model achieved 
an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 
0.805, demonstrating strong discriminative performance. 
Higher C-MELD score, extreme GRWR values (<0.85 or 
>1.35), advanced donor age, and preoperative ventilator 
support emerged as the most influential predictors of EAF 
risk. 
Conclusion(s): By integrating explainable machine 
learning with comprehensive preoperative evaluation, 
this model provides a practical and clinically applicable 
approach for early identification of high-risk recipients.

critical decisions in donor selection and surgical planning. 
Ultimately, such tools may contribute to preventing 
catastrophic EAF events and safeguarding both donor 
sacrifice and recipient survival.

A SIMPLE PRE-TRANSPLANT RISK 
MODEL IDENTIFYING AGE, SMOKING, 
HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA AND 
VASCULAR ISCHEMIC DISEASE AS KEY 
PREDICTORS OF POST-LIVER TRANSPLANT 
MORTALITY 
Maria Senosiain Labiano* 1, 2, Patricia Salvador Bengoechea1, 
2, Eunate Muga Ibarreche1, 2, ander garcia sanmiguel1, 2, alex 
bausela sainz1, 2, Jose Ramón Fernandez ramos1, 2, francisco javier 
bustamante schneider1, 2, arkaitz perfecto valero2, 3, sara mambrilla2, 
3, mikel prieto2, 3, palomares etxeberria2, 3, alberto ventoso 
castañeira2, 3, patricia ruiz ordorica2, 3, mikel gastaca mateo2, 3
1Gastroenterology, Hospital Universitario Cruces, 2Biobizkaia,

Background: The prognostic impact of pre-transplant 
comorbidities on survival after liver transplantation remains 
uncertain. Identifying simple, clinically available predictors 
may improve risk stratification and patient selection.
Purpose: To determine independent predictors of post-
transplant mortality and develop a multivariable Cox model 
suitable for integration into pre-transplant assessment 
workflows. 
Method: A single-centre retrospective cohort of adult liver 
transplant recipients (2014–2021) was analysed. Exclusion 
criteria included retransplantation, acute liver failure, 
combined transplants and ACLF grades 2–3. The primary 
endpoint was all-cause mortality. Candidate predictors 
included age, MELD, sex, aetiology, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, 
hypertension, cardiac, respiratory and vascular comorbidities, 
prior malignancy, chronic kidney disease, smoking status 
and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Model development 
followed a structured process: bivariate screening (p≤0.25), 
correlation and collinearity evaluation, multivariable Cox 
modelling with backward elimination, and comparison of 
nested models using AIC, BIC, C-index and Brier score. 
Result(s): A total of 508 patients were included (median 
follow-up was 80.8 months (IQR 59.6–104.6); 90 deaths 
occurred during follow-up. Age >65 years and current 
smoking emerged as independent predictors across all 
models. The optimal model combined age category (>65 
vs ≤65), smoking status, HCC and vascular ischemic disease 
(defined as the combined presence of ischemic heart disease 
and/or peripheral or abdominal vascular disease). Hazard 
ratios (HR, 95% CI) were: age >65 years 1.85 (1.17–2.94); 
current smoking 2.26 (1.22–4.19); former smoking 1.63 
(0.86–3.09); HCC 1.50 (0.97–2.31); vascular ischemic disease 
1.60 (0.87–2.96). The model achieved a C-index of 0.625 
and favourable AIC/BIC values compared with alternative 
specifications. 
Conclusion(s): Age >65 years and active smoking are strong 
predictors of post-transplant mortality. HCC and vascular 
ischemic disease add additional prognostic information. 
These variables are objective, easily obtainable during pre-
transplant evaluation and may support the development of 
practical prediction tools to enhance risk stratification.

INTRODUCTION
Early Allograft Failure (EAF) is defined as death or retransplantation 
within 90 days after liver transplantation, is a devastating complication
after living donor liver transplantation(LDLT) that occurs in 5.5–7.6% of 
cases. In LDLT, EAF is particularly critical, as a healthy donor is exposed to 
surgical risk, raising clinical and ethical concerns. However, existing models 
rely mainly on postoperative variables, limiting clinical utility and 
underscoring the need for preoperative risk prediction.
OBJECTIVE
This study aimed to develop an explainable artificial intelligence (AI)–
based model for preoperative prediction of EAF in LDLT recipients using 
only pretransplant variables.
METHOD
Study Design and Population
• Retrospective LDLT cohort (IRB No. S2025-1475-0002)
• From January 2006 to January 2021
• Adult recipients (≥18 years) with pretransplant data
• Excluded: retransplantation, dual-donor LDLT, pediatric cases 
Model Development and Validation
• Pretransplant variables: 40 Recipient, donor, and graft-related variables
• Model: XGBoost with stratified 3-fold cross-validation
• Model Interpretation: SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations)
RESULTS
Baseline Characteristics
• A total of 4,272 patients were 
included, with EAF occurring in 
109 patients (2.55%)
• Recipient mean age was 53.2 
years, and donor mean age was 
28.2 years
• MELD score was higher in the 
EAF group (p<0.001)
CONCLUSIONS
• Model Performance: The pretransplant 
explainable AI–based model achieved 
measurable predictive accuracy (AUROC 
0.74, AUPRC 0.11), significantly exceeding 
the baseline prevalence (2.55%).
• Predictive Factors: SHAP identified key 
risks across recipient, donor, and graft 
factors. Notably, GRWR’s non-linear effect 
suggests that graft size alone is insufficient, 
and larger grafts may not fully compensate for 
advanced recipient severity.
• Clinical Implications: These findings 
support an integrated preoperative risk 
assessment incorporating recipient, donor, 
and graft factors for EAF prediction in LDLT.

in Living Donor Liver Transplantation
Key Predictors
• Recipient-related factors: Higher 
procalcitonin, C-reactive protein, 
and MELD score; lower hemoglobin; 
and preoperative mechanical 
ventilation were associated with 
increased predicted risk
• Donor-related factors: Older donor 
age were associated with higher 
predicted risk
• Graft-related factors: GRWR 
showed a non-linear association 
with predicted risk.
Predictive Performance
• On the test sets, AUROC was 0.74 ± 0.02, with 
consistent ROC curves across folds
• AUROC, Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and PPV were 
0.11 ± 0.01, 0.86 ± 0.08, 0.44 ± 0.13, 0.87 ± 0.08, and 
0.10 ± 0.03, respectively.
